result.title: I.  Introduction
result.summary: SFERS administers a defined-benefit pension fund worth approximately $34 billion as of June 30, 2022. Its seven-member Retirement Board has fiduciary authority over investments and system administration, meets monthly in public to set policy, review performance, and consider opportunities, and acts under applicable laws and Board policies solely for members and beneficiaries. SFERS seeks qualified investment consulting firms to advise the Board and staff on total-fund policy and asset allocation, governance, triennial asset-liability studies, annual capital-markets research, risk management, liquidity planning, and ongoing policy implementation and oversight; quarterly performance reporting and benchmark analysis; and Board meeting attendance, education, and training. Selected firms must demonstrate relevant institutional experience, provide market research and trustee education, work with the Board, CEO/CIO, and investment staff, and acknowledge without qualification in writing their fiduciary status, advising solely in members’ and beneficiaries’ interests. Contracts run three years, with two optional one-year extensions exercisable at SFERS’ sole discretion.

result.title: II. Scope of Work
result.summary: The RFP seeks non-discretionary professional investment consulting services, including total-fund policy and asset-allocation studies, capital-market research, allocation and liquidity analysis, scenario and stress testing, risk management, portfolio construction, diversification, tactical allocation, overlays, leverage, policy implementation, and compliance monitoring. Duties also include quarterly performance and attribution reporting, benchmark evaluation, responding to auditors and actuaries, providing software, Board advice and education, project and operational support, custodial recommendations, research access, timely communication, and reporting staffing changes; consultant-team changes require SFERS approval. The blackout period runs from Board approval through contract execution, completion, or termination of the search, with restricted proposer contacts and specified exceptions. Proposals were due December 15, 2022, by 5 p.m. Pacific, with three hard copies and one electronic copy; late or faxed submissions are rejected. The signed transmittal letter must provide required identification, authority, certifications, disclosures, and acknowledgments. Responses must follow the prescribed format, address qualifications and Appendix A questions, and be complete and clear; incomplete, misleading, or nonconforming proposals may be rejected.

nodes.title: I. Introduction
nodes.summary:
II. Scope of Work
The general scope of work for this RFP is to provide non-discretionary professional investment consulting services. Specifically, the successful Firm must demonstrate superior experience and capability in one or more of the areas described below. The following are examples of the duties that SFERS is seeking:

nodes.title: A. Total Fund Policy and Asset Allocation Duties
nodes.summary: The text outlines consultant duties for total-fund policy and asset allocation: conduct generally triennial asset-allocation and liability studies; provide capital-market research and recommendations, analytical tools for allocation, liquidity forecasting, scenarios and stress testing; support risk management, portfolio construction, diversification, tactical allocation, overlays, leverage, long-term policy and implementation processes; and monitor policy compliance. Performance duties include quarterly Board reporting on total-fund, asset-class and peer/benchmark results, attribution and leverage effects; responding to auditor and actuary questions; evaluating benchmarks; and providing attribution software. Training and client-relations duties include attending Board meetings, advising on investment decisions, providing education, special-project and workshop support, operational assistance, custodial-services recommendations, timely responses, sharing firm research and access to research staff, promptly reporting organizational or staffing changes, and making no consultant-team changes without SFERS approval. Submission requirements introduce a blackout period.

nodes.title: Investment Consulting Duties and Submission Requirements
key_items: 1. Present quarterly investment performance results to the Board
C. Training, Education, and Client Relations Duties; III. Submission Requirements
C. Training, Education, and Client Relations Duties
nodes.summary: The page outlines consulting support for capital-markets assumptions, asset allocation tools, liquidity forecasting, scenario analysis, risk management, portfolio construction, diversification, tactical allocation, overlays, leverage, investment policy, and compliance monitoring. Performance duties include quarterly Board reporting on Fund, asset-class, peer and benchmark results, attribution and leverage effects; responding to auditor and actuary questions; benchmark analysis; and access to performance software. Training and client-relations duties include attending meetings, advising on investment decisions, providing education, project and workshop support, operational and custodial assistance, timely responses, sharing Firm research and staff access, reporting organizational or staffing changes, and making no consultant-team changes without SFERS approval. The page also includes a Submission Requirements heading.

nodes.title: A. Blackout Period
nodes.summary: The SFERS RFP blackout began when the Board approved the RFP on October 20, 2022, and lasts until evaluation is complete and a contract is executed, or the Board ends the search. It applies to the Board, designated Assigned Staff, and Proposers to ensure fair, unbiased evaluation. Proposers must not contact Board members or Assigned Staff by meeting, phone, letter, or email, except for written inquiries submitted under the RFP, SFERS-scheduled evaluation interviews, and Board presentations scheduled as part of evaluation and selection. Other meetings are allowed only for topics unrelated to the RFP, covered services, or a response, with advance written notice of the meeting and its subject from both parties to the SFERS CEO/CIO; the CEO/CIO retains notices and may request written confirmation of topics discussed. The blackout does not prevent existing SFERS service providers from necessary communications and meetings to perform their current engagements. Questions must be submitted in writing under the RFP’s specified procedure.

nodes.title: B. Time and Place for Submission of Proposals
nodes.summary:
B. Time and Place for Submission of Proposals
The deadline for submission of responses is December 15, 2022 at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time.
Submissions must include three (3) completed paper (hard) copies of the response and one full and complete electronic copy of the response by the deadline date and time to: Anna Langs Managing Director, Asset Allocation, Risk Management, Innovative Solutions San Francisco Employees' Retirement System 1145 Market Street, 5th Floor San Francisco, CA 94103-1561 Anna.Langs@sfgov.org
4Late submissions will not be considered. Postmarks will not be considered in judging the timeliness of submissions. Proposals that are submitted by fax will not be considered.

nodes.title: C. Transmittal Letter
nodes.summary: The transmittal letter is an integral part of the proposal and must be signed by someone authorized to bind the Proposer, with that authority stated; unsigned cover letters are rejected. It must provide the Proposer’s contact details and applicable federal and corporate identification numbers; the signer’s and, if different, RFP contact’s names, titles, and phone numbers; willingness to perform the services and fiduciary-duty acknowledgment; confirmation of staff and resources; certification that fees and conditions remain firm for 180 days and prices are genuine and non-collusive; acknowledgment of the RFP schedule and key personnel availability for interviews, site visits, and Board meetings; certification that no SFERS officer, employee, agent, or Board member has a known interest in the contract or proceeds; disclosure of relationships with SFERS Board members or staff; acknowledgment that submissions are public records; and a description of professional relationships with SFERS, California, or its political subdivisions during the prior five years, explaining why they pose no conflict of interest.

nodes.title: D. Format and Content of Proposals
nodes.summary:
D. Format and Content of Proposals
Proposer’s response to this RFP must be organized in the format listed below:
1. Transmittal Letter; 2. Statement demonstrating that the Proposer satisfies the minimum qualifications under Section IV(A) of this RFP and a brief description regarding whether Proposer possesses the desired qualifications under Section IV(B); 3. Response to RFP questions detailed in Appendix A; and 4. Additional information or attachments.
5Completeness, brevity, and clarity are important. Proposers should submit all information requested in this RFP and do so in the specified format. Responses not meeting format requirements or that are incomplete may be rejected. Providing incomplete or misleading data may lead to disqualification of the response.

result.title: IV. Evaluation and Selection Criteria
result.summary: The evaluation criteria require at least one proposed key professional to have 10 years of institutional-client experience. SFERS Assigned Staff and the Board have sole discretion over qualification determinations; proposals that fail to demonstrate the minimum by the submission deadline are non-responsive and ineligible for award. Desired qualifications include sophisticated total-fund asset allocation and risk management (capital-markets forecasting, risk-factor analysis, liquidity and pacing for illiquid assets, and leverage effects); assigned professionals averaging at least 10 years of relevant experience; breadth across asset classes; a record of successful, market-leading recommendations; suitable systems and technology; and current consulting work for at least three clients comparable to SFERS in size and complexity. Allocation, asset-liability modeling, and risk-management capabilities should also include successful multi-asset solutions, innovation, forward-looking analysis, alignment of policy and governance with risk/return targets and liquidity needs, and comprehensive risk management.

result.title: C. Selection Criteria
key_items: Total Fund Investment Policy and Asset Allocation – 60% of Total; Performance Reporting – 20% of Total
Total Fund Investment Policy and Asset Allocation – 60% of Total
Training, Education and Client Relations Duties– 20% of Total
result.summary: Proposals are evaluated on Total Fund Investment Policy and Asset Allocation (60%), Performance Reporting (20%), and Training, Education and Client Relations (20%). Within these areas, personnel/organization and investment-policy capabilities are weighted 40%/60%, performance-reporting personnel/organization and duties 40%/60%, and the final category assigns 5% to fees and service coverage and 15% to training and client relations. Criteria include team and organizational depth, structure, ownership and conflicts; investment-policy and multi-asset expertise, innovation, forward-looking allocation, risk management, and quantitative modeling; and timely, accurate, insightful reporting and industry leadership. Training/client criteria include best practices, innovation, benchmarking, Board and Staff skills, useful educational materials, warranties, custody evaluation, insurance/legal/contracting matters, client service, and ESG. After written review, the Board approves semi-finalists; SFERS may conduct interviews and site visits, and key staff must be available. The Board interviews and approves the recommended finalist, who is expected at the public meeting. Fees matter, but the Board need not select the lowest bidder; it chooses the proposal that best serves SFERS and its members and beneficiaries.

result.title: V. Schedule
key_items: A. Schedule of Events (all dates subject to change)
B. Explanation of Schedule of Events
No exceptions to this deadline will be granted.
result.summary: The schedule, subject to change, runs from RFP issuance and advertising on November 1 through questions due November 15, answers posted November 22, and proposals due December 15, 2022, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific with no exceptions. Reviews occur December–January; due diligence January–February; semifinalist presentations and Board approval are scheduled for March 16, 2023; negotiations and service commencement are planned for April. The RFP will be posted on SFERS’s website and sent to potentially qualified firms; all firms meeting minimum qualifications may apply. Written questions or clarification requests must go to Anna Langs by the question deadline. SFERS may issue website addenda, which proposers must account for, and proposers should rely only on SFERS-issued written information. SFERS may interview semifinalists at its office and may change interview dates. Submissions are public records, though business-confidential material should be marked. After Board approval, staff negotiate with the selected proposer; selection does not accept all proposed terms, and SFERS may move to the next-ranked proposer if negotiations fail.

result.title: VI. Terms and Conditions for Receipt of Proposals
result.summary: Proposers must review the RFP and promptly report errors or ambiguities to SFERS; inquiries and clarification or modification requests go to the designated contact. Objections must be submitted with specific grounds within 10 calendar days of issuance or are waived. SFERS may issue addenda, which proposers must monitor and incorporate. Proposals and prices remain valid for 180 days, must be noncollusive, and may be revised before the deadline only through the original submission method. SFERS may seek clarifications, but need not; its failure to flag defects does not excuse compliance. Proposers bear response costs, and submissions become SFERS property. The section addresses Campaign Reform Ordinance compliance, public inspection of records after award and temporary protection of proprietary financial data, and Chapter 12L reporting by qualifying nonprofits on public access and substantiated complaints, with rejection or termination possible for noncompliance or misrepresentation. SFERS may waive defects, reject, revise, cancel, reissue, use other procurement methods, or abandon the project; no contract is promised. LBEs are encouraged to apply. Chapters 12B and 12C prohibit specified contractor discrimination.

nodes.title: RFP Review, Inquiries, Objections, and Addenda
key_items: A. Errors and Omissions in RFP
nodes.summary: Proposers must review the RFP and promptly report ambiguities, discrepancies, omissions, or errors to SFERS by email, no later than five working days before proposals are due; clarifications or changes will be issued by addendum. RFP inquiries and requests for written clarification or modification must be sent by email or in writing to the designated SFERS contact, Anna Langs. Objections to any RFP provision or legal requirement must be submitted in writing, with specific grounds, within ten calendar days of issuance; otherwise, they are irrevocably waived. SFERS may issue written addenda before the proposal deadline and will post them on its website. Proposers must ensure their proposals reflect all addenda and should check the website frequently, including shortly before the deadline.

nodes.title: E. Term of Proposal
nodes.summary: Proposals remain valid for 180 calendar days after the due date, and prices must be genuine and free of collusion. Proposers may revise submissions before the deadline using the original submission method; revisions must arrive by the due date, which cannot be extended by an announced or started revision. SFERS may request clarifications during evaluation or award without them. SFERS’s failure to flag proposal errors or deviations does not change RFP requirements or excuse compliance. SFERS does not reimburse response costs, and submitted materials become its property for use as it deems appropriate. Proposers must review and comply with the Campaign Reform Ordinance, Section 1.126. Under the Sunshine Ordinance, contract-related records become inspectable after award, subject to temporary protection for certain proprietary financial data; covered information is available on request. Qualifying nonprofits receiving at least $250,000 annually in City or City-administered funds must meet Chapter 12L reporting requirements and include a statement in their proposal; the text ends before specifying its contents.

nodes.title: Proposal Rules and Disclosure Requirements
key_items: G. Errors and Omissions in Proposal
I. Proposer’s Obligations Under the Campaign Reform Ordinance
nodes.summary: Proposal services and prices remain valid for 180 calendar days after the due date and must be genuine, not collusive. Proposers may revise submissions before the deadline using the original submission method; statements or work toward a revision do not extend the deadline. SFERS may request clarifications or award without them. SFERS’s failure to flag proposal errors or omissions does not change the RFP or excuse compliance. Proposers bear their response costs, and submitted materials become SFERS property. Proposers must review and comply with Section 1.126 of the San Francisco Campaign and Governmental Conduct Code; the Ethics Commission can provide information. After award, bids, proposals, contracts, and related communications are open to inspection. Proprietary financial data is protected until the person or organization receives the contract or benefit, after which covered information is available to the public upon request.

nodes.title: K. Public Access to Meetings and Records
nodes.summary: Qualifying nonprofits receiving at least $250,000 annually in City or City-administered funds must meet Chapter 12L reporting rules: proposals must describe efforts to provide public access to meetings and records and summarize substantiated complaints filed in the past two years, including outcomes, or state that none were filed. Noncompliance or material misrepresentation may lead to rejection or contract termination. SFERS reserves the right to waive defects, reject proposals, cancel or reissue the RFP, modify procedures or requirements before the deadline, procure by other means, or abandon the project; issuing the RFP does not promise a contract. No waiver is implied by SFERS’s inaction. Qualified Local Business Enterprises are encouraged to apply, with program details available from the City’s Office of Contract Administration. Administrative Code Chapters 12B and 12C are incorporated and prohibit contractor discrimination in employment, property use, and provision of public benefits.

nodes.title: RFP Rights, Chapter 12L Reporting, and LBE Participation
key_items: L. Reservations of Rights by SFERS
nodes.summary: Proposers must report efforts to comply with Chapter 12L public-access requirements and summarize substantiated complaints filed in the past two years, including each complaint’s disposition; if none were filed, they must say so. Failure to report or material misrepresentation may lead to proposal rejection or contract termination. SFERS reserves the right to correct or waive defects, reject proposals, cancel or reissue the RFP, modify procedures or requirements before the deadline, obtain services by other means, or abandon the project. No waiver is implied by SFERS’s inaction regarding a proposer’s noncompliance. SFERS encourages qualified Local Business Enterprises (LBEs) to apply and directs interested proposers to the City’s Office of Contract Administration website for program details and forms.

nodes.title: O. Chapters 12B and 12C: Nondiscrimination in Employment and Benefits
nodes.summary:
O. Chapters 12B and 12C: Nondiscrimination in Employment and Benefits
The provisions of Chapters 12B and 12C of the San Francisco Administrative Code are incorporated by reference as though fully set forth herein. Those provisions prohibit discrimination by City contractors in employment, the use of property, the provision of public
12accommodations and in the provision of benefits to employees with domestic partners and employees with spouses, and/or between the domestic partners and spouses of such employees.
Please refer to Appendix B regarding the requirements of San Francisco Administrative Code Chapters 12B and 12C.

result.title: VII. Contract Requirements
result.summary: The selected Proposer must sign a contract substantially in the form of Appendix C and provide all required certificates, bonds, and materials on time; otherwise, SFERS may treat the offer as abandoned, select another Proposer or take other action, and seek damages. Referenced San Francisco municipal codes are available online at sfgov.org. Before contract award, Proposers must register as City bidders and complete online supplier approval, including Forms P-25, HRC 12B-101, and IRS W-9. These forms must accompany the proposal or it may be deemed non-responsive and rejected. Proposers who previously submitted them to SFERS need not resubmit unless their answers changed, but should say so in their response. Appendix A responses must use Calibri 11.5-point font with blue text; sample text is provided.

result.title: A. Warranties
result.summary: The RFP asks firms to warrant ongoing E&O insurance and disclose coverage types and amounts; certify response accuracy; state GIPS compliance and SEC registration or exemption (with Form ADV or explanation); confirm direct account management by firm employees; and confirm review of the sample consulting agreement by the firm and its counsel, identifying all requested changes. It also requests details on fiduciary-duty litigation and administrative proceedings, related claims that did not proceed formally, and all lawsuits and administrative proceedings from the past five years, including parties, forums, dates, allegations, involved personnel, case numbers, and status or outcome. Firms must disclose regulatory investigations or enforcement actions and investment-related legal matters involving current or former personnel. Finally, firms must describe domestic-partner employment benefits or state whether they would adopt them if selected.

result.title: C. Organization and Personnel
result.summary: Requests a comprehensive profile of the firm: history and relevant expertise; ownership, affiliates, alliances, ownership percentages, and anticipated structural changes; organization, divisions, staffing, offices, SFERS relationship coverage, and past or expected developments. It covers recruitment, retention, workforce attributes and performance measures, culture and engagement, growth objectives, investment products, assets, managers, and conflict controls. It seeks client counts and account statistics by client type, details of the 20 largest clients, and historical staffing by role, qualifications, and investment experience. It also asks about staff departures and planned staffing changes; professional compensation, incentives, profit-sharing and rationale; hiring requirements and practices; competitive strengths and attribute tradeoffs; and accounts lost since 2015, including size and reasons.

result.title: D. ESG Practices
result.summary:
D. ESG Practices
1. Describe if and how ESG factors are considered in consulting related to strategic and tactical investment planning, sub-asset class structure, and/or on-going investment policy development, implementation and oversight.
2. Describe any dedicated or specialty ESG consulting services the Firm offers related to Total Plan Investment Policy and/or Asset Allocation, including but not limited to, those related to climate change risk and diversity, equity & inclusion.
3. Apart from anything mentioned above, please describe any announced or prospective plans for ESG-related consulting services.

result.title: E. Resources Dedicated to SFERS
result.summary: The section requests details on personnel assigned separately to SFERS asset allocation and performance reporting: each person’s name, title, expected role, location, investment and consulting experience, tenure at the firm, assigned-account count and details, account roles, biography, current client workload, and expected time commitment to SFERS. It also asks how the account team will operate, including lead, backup, and support; procedures for staff departures, unavailability, or reduced capacity; the firm’s experience and capabilities in educating public pension trustees and staff, with recent presentation-material examples; and its ability to undertake trustee- or staff-assigned research projects, with recent examples.

result.title: F. Conflicts of Interests
result.summary: The questionnaire covers conflicts of interest: investment-manager and fund-of-funds relationships and safeguards; discretionary versus non-discretionary clients and assets; broker-dealer status and SEC focus reports; soft dollars; parent-company revenue sources; revenues and benefits from investment managers and brokerage; compensation received from named managers; disclosure of beneficial relationships; conflict policies and safeguards for objective advice; and potential conflicts in representing SFERS, including affiliate, parent, and client activities. It asks about technology capabilities, custom analytical tools, and communications and information-sharing resources. Investment-consulting questions address asset-allocation philosophy and market beliefs; allocation approaches; preventing concentration and over-diversification; defined-benefit plan allocation studies and ongoing review; strategic plan-level leverage, its merits, instruments, client examples, and recommendations; and allocation-model theory, methodology, data inputs, treatment of liabilities, funding levels and contribution changes, and liability-analysis capabilities.

result.title: G. Technology and Communication Resources; H. Investment Consulting
result.summary:
G. Technology and Communication Resources
1. Please describe the Firm’s technology capabilities and relate them to the Firm’s consulting services or products. Do you provide any custom computer-based analytical tools to the Firm’s clients? If so, please elaborate.
2. Please describe the Firm’s communication technology capabilities. How does the Firm use technology to share and leverage information resources across the organization?
H. Investment Consulting

result.title: a. Asset Allocation and Modeling
result.summary: The questions seek the Firm’s asset-allocation philosophy, market beliefs, preferred investment approach, and methods for avoiding portfolio concentration or over-diversification. They ask about experience conducting defined-benefit plan allocation studies, including frequency, follow-up, and relevant factors; strategic plan-level leverage, its merits, approaches and instruments, client examples, and a leverage recommendation. They also cover asset-allocation model theory, methodology and inputs, and how liabilities, funding levels, contribution changes, and liability analysis are addressed. The Firm is asked to define total-fund risk and describe monitoring tools and whether they are in-house or third-party. Finally, it should provide a generic public-plan allocation and the information needed for a specific recommendation, and explain how liabilities and liquidity inform allocation decisions, including the models used (such as stochastic, deterministic, or scenario analysis).

result.title: b. Capital Markets Outlook
result.summary: The section requests the Firm’s market-monitoring and reporting capabilities, examples of original capital-markets research, and perspectives on the past 20 years, including emerging markets, technology and credit bubbles, the GFC, and COVID-19. It asks for current market views, risks, opportunities, and strategies concerning equity valuations, credit spreads, inflation/deflation, interest rates and yield curves, real estate, commodities, political instability, climate warming, and economic growth. It seeks capital-markets assumption methods, research inputs, analytical tools, and experience across economic research, asset/liability modeling, allocation, public and private investments, real assets, hedge funds, risk, stress testing, liquidity, and leverage. Respondents should provide intermediate and long-term return and volatility forecasts by asset class, compare expectations with peers and consensus, address scenario-based assumptions and plan risk appetite, and substantiate forecast accuracy across cycles. Finally, it asks about portfolio de-risking, low future fixed-income returns, illiquid allocations and pension liquidity, and an assessment of SFERS’ allocation, expected return and risk, and potential improvements.

result.title: c. Consulting Approach and Investment Policy
result.summary: The text asks about the Firm’s approach to generating differentiated investment ideas, with examples, and about unsuccessful recommendations and lessons learned. It seeks details on monitoring compliance with investment policies and reporting portfolio allocation, characteristics, and risk; common mistakes by consultants, plan sponsors, staff, pension plans, and Boards; and steps to prevent or minimize those mistakes, including risk-management recommendations. It asks how the Firm expects to add value to SFERS over three to five years across areas such as asset allocation, risk management, cost containment, and education, with estimated improvement ranges, and how to measure the Firm’s consulting performance. It also requests the Firm’s approach to developing an Investment Policy Statement (IPS), key considerations, and its public defined-benefit plan experience and capabilities in developing or reviewing investment guidelines. Specifically, it asks what the Firm would do for SFERS, how often reviews should occur, and how IPS implementation and ongoing review are handled.

result.title: I. Performance Analytics
result.summary: The request seeks details on performance measurement, reporting, calculation controls and timeliness; universe and benchmark comparisons, including custom benchmarks; analytics and consolidated reporting across asset classes; online, tailored and custom reports, samples, and delivery timelines; net-of-fee methods and expense basis; investment-compliance monitoring; derivative and leverage handling; loading and maintaining historical performance; lagged and non-lagged private investment returns; daily estimates; monthly manager-versus-custodian market-value and return comparisons, variance explanations and reconciliation; and AB 2833 AIV fee disclosures with samples. It also requests investment education and training materials, client workshops and projects, research and white papers, and information, leadership biographies, services, sample evaluations, and update processes for any global-custodian research team. A single fee quote is requested for all Section II services. Additional electronic materials include an organization chart covering the firm, parent and affiliates; staff biographies; annual report; mission, values and ethics statements; conflict policies; latest SEC Form ADV Parts I and II; and standard marketing brochure.

result.title: Reporting, Client Education, Custodian Research, and Fees
key_items: J.   Training, Education, and Client Relations Duties
result.summary: Requests comparisons of public-market managers’ reported market values and returns with SFERS custodian figures for the latest month and trailing periods, plus explanations of material return differences and reconciliation steps. Asks whether the firm provides annual AIV fee disclosures under California Assembly Bill 2833 and requests a sample. Training and client-relations requests include examples of education materials, client projects and workshops, research and white papers, and details on any global-custodian research team: its size, leadership qualifications, services, sample evaluations, and process for tracking service enhancements. The fee proposal must quote one fee covering all services in the Scope of Work.

result.title: L.  Requested Materials and Additional Information
key_items: J. Training, Education, and Client Relations Duties
result.summary:
L. Requested Materials and Additional Information
In addition to any materials requested in the questions listed above, please send electronic versions of the following documents:
1. A corporate organization chart (showing the consulting Firm, parent and all affiliates and subsidiaries). 2. The biographies of the Firm’s professional staff, including education, investment and consulting experience, and the year they joined the Firm. 3. A current company Annual Report. 4. A copy of the Firm’s mission statement, statement of values, and code of ethics. 5. Current Firm policies related to conflicts-of-interest. 6. Most recently filed SEC Form ADV, Parts I and II. 7. A copy of the Firm’s standard marketing brochure that describes the Firm’s processes and services.
278. Any other information you feel would be necessary to gain a complete understanding of the Firm or the services it provides.

result.title: M.  References
result.summary: Requires references for at least five current clients, five investment managers able to discuss manager research, and three former clients. Each must include organization and contact details and relationship length and asset size; client references also describe services. Missing references are nonresponsive, and unavailability of three former clients must be explained. Appendix B identifies City vendor forms: W-9, P-25, HRC Form 12B-101, and any circumstance-dependent additional forms. Appendix C provides a template nondiscretionary investment consulting agreement, including selection, qualifications, term and extension options, services, fees, fiduciary and disclosure obligations, conflicts, personnel, independent-contractor status, insurance, indemnification, confidentiality, intellectual property, audits, assignment, claims, defaults, termination, and post-termination duties. It also addresses City and other legal and policy compliance, notices, disputes, governing law and venue, amendments, interpretation, severability, and execution.

nodes.title: M.  References (intro)
nodes.summary:
M. References
1. Provide the organization name, address, contact name and title, contact telephone number and email address for at least five existing clients. Indicate the length of your relationship, nature of the services provided, and asset size for each reference. Not including references will be considered non-responsive.
2. Provide the organization name, address, contact name and title, contact telephone number and email address at least five investment managers who can discuss your manager research. Indicate the length of your relationship and asset size for each reference. Not including references will be considered non-responsive.
3. Provide the organization name, address, contact name and title, contact telephone number and email address for three former clients. Indicate the length of your relationship, nature of the services provided, and asset size for each former client listed. Not including references will be considered non-responsive. If three accounts are not available, please explain why.

nodes.title: APPENDIX B
nodes.summary: Appendix B lists required vendor forms, available through the City’s Office of Contract Administration website. Before doing business with the City, vendors must submit: IRS Form W-9, which supplies a taxpayer ID for assignment of a five-digit City vendor number; Form P-25, used to determine whether the vendor does business in San Francisco and owes business taxes; and HRC Form 12B-101, used to assess employee and benefits information for nondiscrimination compliance. Additional forms may be required depending on the vendor’s circumstances. Appendix C provides the opening of a general investment consulting agreement between the Retirement System and a consultant. Its recitals describe the Retirement Board’s investment authority, the goal of retaining nondiscretionary consulting services, selection through an RFP process, and the consultant’s qualification representations. The initial term is specified by dates and may be extended at the Retirement System’s sole discretion through two one-year options, subject to Section 8.

nodes.title: General Investment Consulting Agreement
key_items: SAN FRANCISCO CITY AND COUNTY EMPLOYEES’ RETIREMENT SYSTEM
nodes.summary: Appendix C provides a form agreement between the San Francisco City and County Employees’ Retirement System and a blank-named consultant, with blank execution and term dates. The recitals describe the Retirement System’s establishment, the Retirement Board’s investment and administrative authority and fiduciary responsibility, and the System’s aim to obtain nondiscretionary investment consulting services. They note the RFP and competitive selection process, Board approval of the consultant based on its representations, and the consultant’s representation that it is qualified. The agreement is made in consideration of mutual promises and covenants. Its term is subject to Section 8 and may be extended at the Retirement System’s sole and absolute discretion through two one-year options.

Appendix C is a template agreement between the San Francisco Employees’ Retirement System and an investment consultant for non-discretionary portfolio advice, governed by the Investment Policy Statement, service schedule, applicable law, and a term with two optional one-year extensions. It covers authorized services, fees and annual caps, payment approval, quarterly invoicing, budget appropriations, fiduciary standards, adviser registration and disclosures, conflicts, personnel, and limits on tax/legal advice. It sets requirements for independent-contractor status, taxes, insurance, indemnification, confidentiality, intellectual property ownership, audit access, and restrictions on assignment or subcontracting. It establishes false-claims liability, defaults and remedies, discretionary termination, post-termination duties, and prohibited conflicts, gifts, and salary-history practices. It requires compliance with City and other laws and policies concerning nondiscrimination, labor, hiring, contributions, political activity, accessibility, public records, and workplace conduct. It also addresses notices, disputes, California law and venue, amendments, entire agreement, construction, severability, cooperative drafting, counterparts, and execution.

result.title: Introduction
result.summary: The Investment Policy Statement (IPS) establishes the framework for managing San Francisco City and County Employees’ Retirement System assets and helps the Retirement Board supervise and monitor the Plan. It covers investment goals and beliefs, management policies and procedures, strategic asset allocation, rebalancing, asset-class definitions, and responsible parties’ duties. Adopted under applicable local, state, and federal law, the policy is set by the Board and executed by Investment Staff with delegated discretion. The Board’s fiduciary principles require it to prioritize participants and beneficiaries, provide benefits exclusively for them, minimize contributions, and pay reasonable administrative expenses; act with prudent-expert care, skill, and diligence; and diversify Plan assets to balance risk and return. Diversification applies to the portfolio overall and does not prohibit concentrated investment styles. The IPS also provides flexibility to pursue investment opportunities while setting reasonable safeguards for prudent implementation.

result.title: Investment Goals
result.summary: SFERS aims to provide legally required retirement benefits through a planned, long-term investment program. Over a full market cycle, its annualized net-of-fee portfolio return should exceed the current 7.4% actuarial assumption and, over rolling five-year periods, the policy-based benchmark. Transactions must exclusively benefit members and beneficiaries while minimizing plan contributions and covering reasonable administrative costs. Asset allocation should reflect long-term capital markets, plan liabilities, and effects on employee and employer contributions; SFERS views consistent, disciplined implementation as the main driver of performance. Investment decisions and policies must meet prudent-expert standards.

result.title: Investment Beliefs
result.summary:
INVESTMENT BELIEFS
1. Investment plan design should reflect a long-term horizon.
2. The power of compound returns and capital preservation is substantial and should be recognized.
3. Volatility in the short term can be substantial but diminishes over long periods of time.
4. Reducing the potential for investment loss that leads to increased employer and employee contributions is a priority.
5. Asset allocation is the primary determinant of risk and return.
6. Investment decisions should be made in a total portfolio context.
7. Superior returns are achieved through asset allocation, asset rebalancing, and manager and security selection.
8. Material environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors can affect the risk and return characteristics of investments.
D-19. To achieve its mission, SFERS seeks to partner with exceptional managers with identifiable investment skill and ability to recognize and exploit less efficient market segments.
10. Specialist managers tend to outperform generalists.

result.title: Investment Policies and Procedures
result.summary: SFERS’s investment policies seek total returns while balancing capital preservation and risk-adjusted performance. Asset allocation reflects actuarial needs, markets, economic outlook and funding status; it diversifies assets, sets target ranges, and is monitored and revised, with ESG integrated subject to fiduciary duties. The section establishes manager selection, evaluation and termination criteria, delegated duties, consultant roles, emerging-business participation, custody review, and controls on derivatives, shorting, leverage and credit facilities. It defines asset classes, purposes, strategies and return objectives; rebalancing triggers, approvals, exceptions and reporting; and public-equity and fixed-income rules for benchmarks, eligible investments, cash, hedging, liquidity, exposure and tracking error. It assigns oversight and implementation responsibilities to the Board, Staff, managers, custodian and consultants, including due diligence, monitoring, compliance, accounting, performance and reporting. An appendix sets allocation targets, ranges and benchmarks, including composite and interim benchmarks.

nodes.title: Investment Policies and Procedures (intro)
nodes.summary: SFERS manages assets for total return, balancing capital preservation and risk-adjusted returns. Asset allocation reflects actuarial needs, markets, economic outlook and funding status; it diversifies assets, permits target ranges, and is monitored and periodically revised. ESG is integrated consistently with fiduciary duties. Managers are selected under applicable laws and contracts, must meet tailored experience, registration, stability, size, style, fee and reporting criteria, and are regularly assessed against benchmarks and guidelines; termination may follow specified performance, compliance, personnel, ethical, cooperation, confidence or strategy concerns. Managers have delegated discretion and fiduciary duties; consultants advise, monitor and report but generally lack discretion. SFERS seeks qualified emerging-business services where prudent. Assets are held by a master custodian, reviewed at least every five years. Derivatives, shorts and leverage require written authorization and controls; derivatives cannot exceed guidelines or be speculative unless allowed. Total-plan leverage targets 3% (0–5%), with monitoring, collateral and exposure limits. Credit facilities require Board/consultant approval, loans below $600 million, CIO and Executive Director authorization, and regular reporting.

nodes.title: ASSET ALLOCATION INVESTMENT GUIDELINES AND REBALANCING PROCEDURES
nodes.summary: Defines SFERS asset classes, purposes, strategies and return objectives: growth (public/private equity), income (credit, Treasuries, cash), diversifiers (real estate, natural resources, infrastructure) and absolute return. Rebalancing rules cover triggers, approvals, considerations, temporary exceptions and monthly Board reporting. Public equity guidelines address management, benchmarks, eligible securities, cash, currency hedging, liquidity, long/short exposure and tracking error; fixed income covers Treasury and liquid-credit portfolios, eligible instruments, derivatives and exception approvals. The section assigns governance and responsibilities: the Board sets and reviews policy, allocation, performance, costs and oversight; Staff implements policy, rebalances, conducts due diligence and manager, consultant, custodian, lending and risk oversight, research and reporting; managers follow guidelines, communicate changes and reconcile data; the master custodian provides custody, accounting, performance, compliance and related services; consultants advise, monitor and report. The allocation appendix gives targets, ranges and benchmarks, including the total-fund composite and interim benchmark arrangements.

nodes.title: Asset Class Definitions
nodes.summary: SFERS’ strategic allocation uses composite benchmarks to assess asset-class risk/returns, estimate expected returns, and define public-market investable universes. Growth is the main return and volatility source: diversified US, developed ex-US, emerging-market, global, and opportunistic public equities may use active or passive strategies, with currency hedging permitted; private equity uses buyout, venture, growth, special-situations and opportunistic investments, targeting at least 300 basis points above public equity over rolling 10-year periods. Income provides yield, stability, downside protection and diversification through private credit (targeting a 150-basis-point premium over liquid credit), diversified liquid credit, Treasuries, and cash. Cash covers benefits and expenses (target three months; range one–four), investment liquidity (target 0%, maximum 5%), and cash overlays using futures to reduce rebalancing costs. Diversifying assets hedge inflation and reduce traditional-market correlation: private real estate, natural resources and opportunistic infrastructure seek income and alpha. Absolute return seeks low-volatility, low-correlation returns, capital preservation and alpha through diversified global equity, credit, macro, emerging-market, quantitative, multi-strategy, special-situations and commodity exposures.

nodes.title: Rebalancing
nodes.summary: Rebalancing is conducted regularly when allocation ranges are breached, cash flows occur, or other circumstances warrant it in the Plan’s and beneficiaries’ best interests, to keep allocations within Appendix ranges. The CIO, supported by Managing Directors, oversees broad asset-class rebalancing. Senior Portfolio Managers and Directors recommend actions to the relevant Managing Director and implement them with CIO approval. Decisions consider cash needs, allocations versus targets and ranges, market conditions, and managers’ performance and other attributes. Broad asset-class breaches are corrected to within Appendix ranges; Staff may also redeploy assets within an asset class, subject to Managing Director and CIO approval. Ranges may remain breached temporarily when suitable managers are unavailable, Staff oppose adding assets to existing managers, or market conditions are unfavorable. The CIO reports monthly to the Board on rebalancing activity and policy exceptions.

nodes.title: Public Market Equity
nodes.summary: The public equity portfolio is managed for total return using varied styles through SMAs and/or commingled funds. Allocations are assessed against pre-established benchmarks in SMA guidelines and, where applicable, similar-style manager peers; benchmarks may be adjusted to exclude restricted stocks. Cash is capped at 10% unless guidelines allow more. Exchange- or NASDAQ-listed depositary receipts and convertible securities are permitted when authorized, with convertibles treated as equities. Securities must trade on regulated exchanges, NASDAQ, or comparable foreign markets; up to 5% may be in private securities. Currency forwards or futures are allowed only in designated currency-overlay portfolios for hedging or pending investment selection or settlement. Liquidity guidelines require at least 25% available within one month and limit holdings taking over 12 months to 15%. Long/short strategies are permitted. Portfolio exposure targets are 75–100% net long, 75–150% gross long, and 0–50% gross short. Expected tracking error is 3%, within a 1–5% range.

nodes.title: Public Market Fixed Income Portfolios
nodes.summary: Public Market Fixed Income consists of separate U.S. Treasury and Liquid Credit allocations. Treasuries provide diversified exposure to the Treasury market; Liquid Credit is managed for total return across specific styles or multiple fixed-income sectors. Allocations may use separately managed accounts or commingled funds and are evaluated against preselected benchmarks in written SMA guidelines and, where applicable, peer managers with similar styles. Permissible securities depend on each manager’s style and risk-return objectives and may include government and agency bonds, corporate and convertible bonds, floating-rate loans, securitized assets, and cash equivalents. Derivatives may manage risk, enhance returns, or support timely, cost-effective portfolio decisions; short positions are allowed. Exceptions require approval from the CIO, Managing Director for Asset Allocation, Risk Management, and Innovative Solutions, and General Consultant, and must be reported to the Board. The text then introduces a section on duties of responsible parties.

nodes.title: Duties of the SFERS Board
nodes.summary: The SFERS Board sets the investment policy framework, while Staff implements and administers its decisions. At least every three years—or sooner after material, lasting changes—the Board reviews investment structure, asset allocation, and performance, including strategic allocation adjustments for regulatory, market, actuarial, or financial changes. It reviews results at least quarterly, monitoring absolute and benchmark- and peer-relative returns using information from Staff, consultants, the custodian, performance providers, and managers. The Board may retain investment consultants for performance and manager reviews, allocation, and research, considering their advice alongside other information and Staff’s recommendations when selecting consultants. It must act when objectives or guidelines are not met, direct cost-effective investment administration subject to Board approval, select a qualified custodian with Staff’s advice (and consultants’ advice when directed), and oversee Staff’s implementation of policy. Investment costs include management, consulting, custodial, transaction, and other SFERS administrative expenses.

nodes.title: Duties of the Investment Staff
nodes.summary: SFERS Investment Staff implements and administers Board policy, while the Board monitors staff performance. Duties include managing funds under written policies, rebalancing, assessing risk, conducting due diligence and making investment recommendations. Staff monitors external managers for guideline and contract compliance, information quality, ability to meet objectives, material organizational or strategy changes, and benchmark and peer-group performance; managers must report material changes. Staff oversees consultant relationships and recommends consultant retention, conducts manager searches, and manages portfolio restructurings after terminations. Staff also conducts or directs research, reviews custodian cost-effectiveness and performance at least every five years, and monitors securities lending and credit facilities, reporting annually on their performance/activity/initiatives and cost/utilization/initiatives, respectively. With the General Investment Consultant, Staff reports on leverage-program use and results. With consultants, Staff presents annual Board updates on asset allocation and risk, ESG, public fixed income and equity, absolute return, private credit, real assets, and private equity, covering strategy, co-investment/direct investment, performance as appropriate, activity, and initiatives. Private equity, real assets, and private credit performance are reviewed annually.

nodes.title: Duties of the Investment Managers
nodes.summary: Investment Managers must agree in writing to follow the Plan’s guidelines, provide annual proof of liability and fiduciary insurance, and be SEC-registered or exempt while demonstrating sustained expertise managing institutional tax-exempt assets in their specialty. They must follow their assigned investment style, including strategy development, research, and securities trading; execute Plan-benefiting transactions through qualified institutional brokers at best net cost; and reconcile monthly accounting, transaction, and asset data with custodian valuations, resolving significant discrepancies. They must maintain frequent, open communication with the System about material matters, including changes in outlook, strategy, portfolio structure, ownership, organization, finances, or assigned personnel; qualifying client terminations (within 30 days when the client represents at least 5% of firm AUM or 10% of the relevant strategy’s assets); other significant investment-process issues; and meet with Staff or the Board as needed.

nodes.title: Duties of the Master Custodian
nodes.summary: The Master Custodian must provide global custody and depository services; manage a Board-directed short-term investment fund and invest available cash in approved vehicles, cooperating with external cash managers when applicable; report monthly investment activity and portfolio performance; collect income and principal, process tax reclaims, and maintain accounting records. It must deliver timely monthly and year-end transaction statements using accurate cost and market values, alert SFERS Staff to uncertain pricing, valuation, or accrued income, and provide performance attribution, guideline and investment-style compliance checks, and calculations conforming to CFA Institute GIPS. It must reconcile valuations and price variances monthly with investment managers and assist with audits, proxy voting, transaction verification, and other Board-requested matters. If directed, it must manage securities lending and related cash collateral, cooperate with external lending agents, and offer credit-facility options for liquidity management.

nodes.title: Duties of the Investment Consultants
nodes.summary: Consultants are selected under applicable law, serve as co-fiduciaries under formal contracts, generally lack discretion, provide timely investment-policy recommendations, monitor managers, report quarterly, and follow CFA Institute ethics and conduct standards. The Board and Staff consider their advice alongside other information. The General Consultant supports policy and asset-allocation decisions; public-manager selection, guidelines and oversight; custodian and credit-facility selection when directed; quarterly leverage and performance reporting; annual co-investment/direct-investment reporting; and relevant research, education and other requested work. Private-market consultants advise on policy, allocation, manager selection and oversight (including related public managers), prepare annual class updates, and provide research, education and requested support. The allocation appendix sets targets/ranges: growth 60% (45–75%), including public equity 37%, private equity 23%; diversifying assets 20% (real assets and absolute return 10% each); income 23% (15–30%), including liquid credit 5%, private credit 10%, and Treasuries 8%; cash 0% (0–5%). It specifies asset-class index benchmarks and a total-fund composite weighted by targets (103%, range 100–105%). Targets were approved November 10, 2020; an interim benchmark uses November 30 allocations plus subsequent private-market and absolute-return deployment, with the General Consultant recognizing transition changes.
